NEW PATIENT - establishing care

65M, retired construction foreman (ran crews for a commercial builder, mostly steel and concrete), here to take over primary care from his old office. Brought a bag of bottles. Old records requested, not here yet, so history is mostly from him and the bottles.

He has had sugar for about ten years, pressure longer than that. Has had AF for years and has been on warfarin the whole time; INRs were done at an outside lab with phone calls from the old office and he says nobody ever called back. Had a mild stroke in 2017, a few days in the hospital, fully recovered with no lingering problems. That's what made him quit smoking. Told he has blockages in the leg arteries a year or two ago, no claudication he can point to. Reflux controlled on omeprazole. Sees an outside cardiologist once a year for the AF.

Meds (verified with bottles):
- metformin 1000 mg BID
- lisinopril 20 mg daily
- HCTZ 12.5 mg daily
- metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily
- warfarin 5 mg daily, adjusted per INR
- aspirin 81 mg daily
- atorvastatin 40 mg daily
- omeprazole 20 mg daily

Allergies: NKDA

Family: father died at 72 of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. Mother had type 2 diabetes and macular degeneration. Paternal uncle had Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia. Brother with high blood pressure.

Social: married, lives in Florence. Smoked about 40 pack-years, quit 2017. Glass of red wine with dinner most nights, no more than that. Walks the dog, putters in the garage.

ROS: no chest pain, no shortness of breath, no palpitations he notices, no leg pain with walking, no bleeding problems on warfarin, no heartburn on the PPI. Otherwise negative.

Exam: well appearing, heavyset. Heart irregularly irregular, rate controlled, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen obese, soft, nontender. Feet: skin intact, DP pulses palpable but faint bilaterally, monofilament intact. Neuro grossly nonfocal, symmetric grip, steady gait.

A/P:
1. T2DM - on metformin. A1c, UACR today. Eye exam is with an outside eye doctor yearly; will request.
2. HTN - acceptable today on lisinopril/HCTZ. CMP.
3. Permanent AF on warfarin, hx of stroke 2017 - continue metoprolol and warfarin. We will manage INRs here going forward: INR today, then about monthly, RN to call results. Keeps his yearly cardiology visit.
4. HLD - atorvastatin 40, lipids today.
5. PAD - aspirin, statin. Asked old office for any vascular studies.
6. GERD - stable on omeprazole.
7. Obesity - BMI over 30, talked about portions and walking more.
8. Former smoker, 40 pk-yr, quit 2017 - discussed annual low-dose CT screening, he is in favor. Ordered.
9. HM - Hep C and HIV screening today. Flu and shingles vaccine at a nurse visit next month. Will look for colonoscopy and tetanus dates in records.

RTC 3 months, INR monthly.

documents.title: Vascular surgery consultation
documents.author: vascular surgery
documents.body:
OUTSIDE VASCULAR SURGERY - new patient consultation. Date of service 09/06/2022.

Reason: infrarenal AAA found on exam and ultrasound by his primary care physician.

Mr. Rossi is a 68 year old retired foreman with AF on warfarin, prior mild ischemic stroke, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia and mild PAD. Asymptomatic: no abdominal or back pain. Former 40 pack-year smoker. His father died of a ruptured AAA at 72, which weighs heavily on him.

Medications: metformin, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, metoprolol succinate, warfarin, aspirin, atorvastatin, omeprazole. Allergies: none known.

Exam: Pulsatile, nontender supraumbilical mass. Femoral pulses palpable bilaterally. Distal pulses present.

CTA 9/2: fusiform infrarenal AAA 4.8 cm, good neck, iliacs normal caliber - favorable for EVAR. Creatinine 1.0.

Assessment and plan: 4.8 cm infrarenal AAA. We discussed that in men repair is usually offered at 5.5 cm and that surveillance imaging every 6-12 months is reasonable. Given his strong family history and his own preference after a long discussion, we will proceed with elective EVAR, scheduled 9/26. Hold warfarin 5 days before (last dose 9/20), no bridging needed; continue aspirin. Hold metformin the day of the procedure. Plan to resume warfarin the day after.

Thank you for this referral.

OUTSIDE HOSPITAL DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 10/10/2022, discharged 10/14/2022. Service: Vascular Surgery.

Principal diagnosis: cholesterol embolism syndrome after EVAR, with acute kidney injury and lower extremity skin involvement.

History: 68 year old man seen two weeks after elective EVAR (9/26) with a creatinine that had climbed on outpatient labs and new mottling of both legs with painful, bluish toes. Baseline creatinine 1.0.

Exam on admission: lacy livedo reticularis over both lower legs and thighs; toes tender with bluish discoloration; pedal pulses present. Groin access sites healed.

Data: creatinine 1.8 on admission, peak 1.9 on 10/12, 1.6 at discharge. Eosinophils 9%. Urinalysis with a few white cells and no significant proteinuria. Skin punch biopsy of the left calf: cholesterol clefts within small dermal arterioles.

Course: supportive care with IV fluids and avoidance of further contrast and catheter procedures. Metformin held while in hospital and resumed at discharge as creatinine improved. Statin and other home medications continued. Toes less tender by discharge; livedo persists.

Allergies: NKDA.
Discharge medications: unchanged from admission list - metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, warfarin 5 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily.

Follow-up: PCP within one week with BMP. Vascular surgery clinic with duplex in about 5 weeks.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Post-discharge visit. Discharge summary and path reviewed.

Admitted 10/10-10/14 to vascular surgery with cholesterol embolism two weeks after his EVAR: AKI (Cr 1.0 baseline, peak 1.9, 1.6 at discharge), eosinophils 9%, livedo on both legs and blue tender toes, skin biopsy with cholesterol clefts. Supportive care.

Today: toes much less sore, he can wear his work boots again. Legs still blotchy but fading. Urinating normally. Appetite ok. Taking all meds, metformin back on since discharge.

Exam: Livedo reticularis faint over both shins and thighs. Toes warm, color better, still a little tender. DP pulses present. Groins healed. Heart irreg irreg. Lungs clear.

Labs today: Cr 1.4, K normal. INR back in range.

A/P:
1. Cholesterol embolism after EVAR with AKI - improving. Recheck BMP in ~6 weeks. Avoid NSAIDs and contrast where possible. Metformin ok at this kidney function; will hold if it goes the other way.

It started as a sense of heavy thighs on stairs. It has worsened to the point that rising from low seats is hard, and he loses his grip on tools or drops things when reaching overhead. No pain, numbness or fasciculations. No injury, infection or medication changes around the onset.

PMH: T2DM, hypertension, permanent AF on warfarin, hyperlipidemia, mild ischemic stroke 2017 fully recovered, GERD, PAD, AAA s/p EVAR 9/2022 with cholesterol embolism.
Meds: metformin, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, metoprolol succinate, warfarin, aspirin, atorvastatin, omeprazole. NKDA.
Family: paternal uncle with Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia; no family neuromuscular disease known.
Social: retired construction foreman, former smoker, a glass of wine most evenings.

Exam: Mild wasting of the quadriceps and the forearm flexors. Weakness in proximal and distal muscles of both arms and both legs. Reflexes normal and symmetric. Light touch, vibration and joint position sense intact. Cranial nerves normal.

Data: CK, electrolytes and TSH from his PCP in December normal. EMG/NCS today nonspecific.

Impression: slowly progressive weakness with a mixed proximal and distal pattern and quadriceps/forearm flexor atrophy. An inflammatory or degenerative myopathy remains the leading concern despite a normal CK.

documents.title: Neurology follow-up

OUTSIDE NEUROLOGY - follow-up. Date of service 03/20/2023.

Reviewed the muscle biopsy with Mr. Rossi: rimmed vacuoles within myofibers. Together with the pattern of weakness (quadriceps and finger/forearm flexors), slow course and nonspecific EMG, this fits inclusion body myositis.

He denies swallowing difficulty at present. Weakness unchanged since February.

Discussion: IBM is slowly progressive, and steroids and other immune treatments have not been shown to help, so we do not recommend them. Focus is on keeping strength and preventing falls: referral to physical therapy for a strengthening and balance program, home safety (rails, raised seats). Report any new choking or trouble swallowing, as IBM can affect swallowing over time.

Diagnosis: inclusion body myositis.
Plan: PT; neurology follow-up in 6-12 months. We asked his PCP to place the PT referral close to home. Thank you.

OUTSIDE CANCER CENTER - medical and radiation oncology consultation. Date of service 09/05/2024.

Diagnosis: adenocarcinoma of the distal esophagus, moderately differentiated.
Staging: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis 8/26 - distal esophageal thickening, no adenopathy or metastasis. PET-CT 8/29 - avid distal esophageal primary, no other avid disease. EUS 9/3 - uT3 N0. Clinical stage cT3 N0 M0.

Relevant history: inclusion body myositis with proximal and distal weakness, permanent AF on warfarin, prior stroke, diabetes, hypertension, PAD, EVAR 2022 complicated by cholesterol embolism. Weight 78 kg, down about 10 lb.

Discussed at multidisciplinary tumor board. Options were chemoradiation followed by esophagectomy, or definitive chemoradiation. Given his age, IBM-related weakness and vascular comorbidity, the board and Mr. Rossi favored definitive chemoradiation with close surveillance.

Plan:
- Weekly carboplatin AUC 2 and paclitaxel 50 mg/m2 with radiation 50.4 Gy in 28 fractions, starting 9/16.
- Ondansetron 4 mg ODT as needed for nausea.
- Dietitian; high-calorie shakes. Feeding tube only if he cannot keep weight up.
- Weekly CBC during treatment; INR more often while on chemotherapy - his PCP's office manages warfarin and will continue.
- Restaging PET-CT and endoscopy about 3 months after completion.

Medications: metformin, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, metoprolol succinate, warfarin, aspirin, atorvastatin, omeprazole. NKDA.

Social: retired construction foreman; 40 pack-years, quit 2017; red wine most evenings.

Exam: pale. Fundoscopy shows engorged retinal veins. Distal sensory loss in both lower extremities. No palpable lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly.

Labs today: hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, MCV 89 fL, platelets 150,000/uL. SPEP with a monoclonal IgM spike, M-protein 3.6 g/dL; IgM 4,850 mg/dL. Serum viscosity elevated at 4.6 cP.

Procedure today: bone marrow aspirate and biopsy, posterior iliac crest, tolerated well (INR checked; warfarin not held, held pressure).

Assessment: monoclonal IgM paraproteinemia with symptomatic hyperviscosity (headache, visual blurring, retinal venous engorgement, mucosal bleeding) and anemia - most consistent with Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, marrow pending.

Plan:
- Plasmapheresis urgently: first session tomorrow 8/12, second 8/14.
- Marrow results expected within the week; definitive therapy to follow.
- Avoid transfusion before plasmapheresis.
- He will continue warfarin; any significant bleeding to the ED.

SPECIMEN: Bone marrow aspirate and core biopsy, posterior iliac crest.
